metricHelp.accuracy: The share of all samples the model got right. It reads easily, but it misleads when one class holds most of the data. For example, if 90 of 100 samples share one class, answering with that class every time already scores 90%. Read it together with the other scores.
metricHelp.f1: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, so a high score on only one of them does not lift it. For example, 90% precision with 10% recall gives an F1 score of 18%. It is worked out for each class, and this model’s F1 score is the average of those.
metricHelp.precision: Of the samples the model answered with this class, the share that really were this class. What matters is the denominator: the model’s own answers. For example, in a factory test it asks how many of the parts pulled aside as faulty really were faulty. A low number means the model reaches for this class too often and throws out good parts with the bad.
metricHelp.recall: Of the samples that really are this class, the share the model found. The denominator is the truth, and that is what separates it from precision. For example, in a factory test it asks how many of the truly faulty parts were caught, because the ones missed ship out. Missing a class and over-using it are different problems, so read the two together.
metricHelp.specificity: Of the samples that are not this class, the share the model correctly kept out of it. For example, in a medical test it is the ability to tell a healthy person they are healthy, and when it is low, healthy people get told they are ill. It is easy to confuse with precision: both catch the same mistake, but precision divides by the model’s answers while specificity divides by every sample that truly is not this class.
metricHelp.support: How many samples of this class the test data really held. It counts the data used for scoring, not the data used for training. When it is small, the scores beside it swing wildly. For example, when it is 3, getting one more right or wrong moves recall by 33 points.
metricHelp.r2: How much of the variation in the values the model explains. Closer to 1 is better, and 0 means it did no better than answering with the average every time. Below that it goes negative.
metricHelp.rmse: How far the predictions land from the real values, and lower is better. Errors are squared before they are added up, so one badly wrong prediction pulls the number up a long way. The unit is the same as the value being predicted: if you predicted a price in dollars, read this in dollars.
metricHelp.mae: How far the predictions land from the real values on average, and lower is better. Every error counts the same, so one badly wrong prediction moves it less. For example, if everything else is close but a single prediction is far off, RMSE climbs sharply while this number barely moves.
metricHelp.silhouette: How well each sample fits its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster, averaged over every sample. It runs from -1 to 1, and the closer to 1, the more clearly the clusters are separated. Around 0 the clusters touch each other, and a negative score means many samples sit closer to a neighboring cluster than to their own.
metricHelp.inertia: The squared distance from every sample to the center of its own cluster, all added up. Lower means tighter clusters, but it always drops as you add more clusters, so it cannot tell you on its own whether the result is good. For example, note the value with 2, 3, and 4 clusters and look for where it stops dropping sharply.

columnHelp.target: The column the model has to guess. You can pick only one, and the column you pick cannot also be a feature. For example, to guess exam scores, the score column is the target. Clustering has no target.
columnHelp.feature: A column the model uses as evidence. You can pick several, and columns you leave unpicked are not used in training. For example, to guess exam scores you might pick study hours and attendance.
columnHelp.kind: Whether this column reads as Numeric or Categorical. Numeric columns go through scaling, categorical ones through encoding. Some columns are written as numbers but have no size meaning, such as a grade level or a postal code, so it is worth checking with your own eyes.
columnHelp.missing: How many rows have no value here. Empty boxes must be either filled in or dropped before training, and you choose which in [Tidy the data] below.
columnHelp.unique: How many different values this column holds. A column with only one value cannot tell anything apart, and a categorical column adds one encoded column per value, so many values means many columns.
columnHelp.effect: What actually happens to this column with the current settings. Filled-in values and scaling are worked out from the training data only, so these numbers are not the whole column.
